items.prompt: Which camera setting is the opening in the lens that controls how much light passes through, and is measured in f-numbers?

options.label: ISO
Aperture
Shutter speed
White balance

rubric: Aperture is the lens opening measured in f-numbers.
Shutter speed is a time setting, and ISO is sensor sensitivity.

items.prompt: What does ISO control on a digital camera?

options.label: The length of time the shutter stays open
The size of the lens opening
The distance at which the lens focuses
The sensor's sensitivity to light

rubric: ISO sets the sensor's sensitivity to light.
Distractors name the jobs of shutter speed, aperture and focus.

items.prompt: Which of these is a typical shutter speed setting?

options.label: ISO 400

rubric: Shutter speed is written as a fraction of a second.
f/2.8 is aperture, ISO 400 is sensitivity and 5600 K is colour temperature.

items.prompt: What is the name of the composition guideline that places the subject along lines dividing the frame into three equal parts?

options.label: Exposure compensation
Golden hour
Rule of thirds
Depth of field

rubric: The rule of thirds splits the frame into a 3x3 grid.
Golden hour is a time of day, and depth of field is about focus range.

items.prompt: Which term describes the range of distance in a photo that appears acceptably sharp?

options.label: Dynamic range
Field of view
Focal length
Depth of field

rubric: Depth of field is the zone of acceptable sharpness.
Field of view is how much scene is captured, which learners often confuse with it.

items.prompt: Which of the following are the three settings of the exposure triangle? Select all that apply.

options.label: Focal length
Aperture
ISO
White balance
Shutter speed

rubric: Aperture, shutter speed and ISO together set exposure.
White balance affects colour, and focal length affects framing.

items.prompt: Maya is new to her camera and wants a quick way to make the whole picture lighter or darker without choosing each setting herself. A friend says there is a control for this that works in steps called stops. Which control is her friend describing?

options.label: Autofocus point selection
Self-timer delay setting
Image format selection
Exposure compensation

rubric: Exposure compensation nudges brightness up or down in stops.
Autofocus point, self-timer and format do not change brightness.

items.prompt: A photographer changes the aperture from f/2.8 to f/8. What happens to the amount of light reaching the sensor, other settings unchanged?

options.label: It decreases, because the lens opening gets smaller
It increases, because more of the scene is in focus
It increases, because the f-number is bigger
It stays the same, because only shutter speed affects light

rubric: A higher f-number means a smaller opening and less light.
Many learners think a larger number means a larger opening.

items.prompt: Why does a very slow shutter speed, such as 1/4 s, often produce blurry photos of people walking when shooting handheld?

options.label: The ISO automatically drops too low to record detail
The lens opening becomes too small to focus
The sensor records movement during the long exposure
The camera cannot judge colour in dim light

rubric: A long exposure records movement of subject or camera as blur.
Distractors link blur to aperture, ISO or colour, which are not the cause.

items.prompt: Why does raising ISO from 100 to 3200 often make a photo look grainy?

options.label: The lens opens wider, which softens the edges
The sensor signal is amplified, which also amplifies noise
The shutter stays open longer, which smears fine detail
The camera compresses the file more, which removes detail

rubric: Higher ISO amplifies the signal along with noise.
Shutter and aperture are separate settings and are not changed by ISO.

items.prompt: Which aperture choice gives a portrait with a blurred background?

options.label: A narrow opening such as f/16
A wide opening such as f/1.8
A low ISO such as 100
A fast shutter such as 1/4000 s

rubric: A wide aperture gives shallow depth of field and blurry backgrounds.
Learners often assume a large f-number means more blur.

items.prompt: A photo taken at midday in bright sun shows harsh, dark shadows on a face. How would you classify this light?

options.label: Backlight from behind the subject
Ambient light with no direction
Soft light from a large, diffused source
Hard light from a small, direct source

rubric: Direct sun is a small source relative to the subject, giving hard shadows.
Soft light needs diffusion such as cloud or a window.

items.prompt: Which of the following explain why a photographer might choose a fast shutter speed such as 1/1000 s? Select all that apply.

options.label: To make the background more blurry
To freeze a running child's motion
To show water as a silky streak
To reduce blur from camera shake with a long lens

rubric: Fast shutters freeze motion and reduce shake blur.
Silky water needs a slow shutter, and background blur comes from aperture.

items.prompt: Tom photographs a friend standing in front of a bright window. His friend's face comes out very dark while the window looks fine. He asks why.

options.label: The ISO was set too high, so the camera lost shadow detail in the face
The shutter speed was too slow, so motion blur darkened the face
The aperture was too wide, so the face fell outside the focus area
The camera exposed for the bright window, so the face was underexposed

rubric: Metering is pulled by the bright window, so the subject is underexposed.
Too-high ISO or slow shutter would brighten, not darken, the face.

items.prompt: You change the aperture from f/8 to f/2.8 and keep the same distance to your subject. What happens to depth of field?

options.label: It stays the same, since only brightness changes
It becomes deeper, so the background gets sharper
It becomes shallower, but only the foreground blurs
It becomes shallower, so the background blurs more

rubric: A wider aperture (smaller f-number) gives shallower depth of field.
Distractors confuse f-number direction or treat aperture as affecting only brightness.

items.prompt: Why do photos taken at a very high ISO often look grainy?

options.label: The shutter stays open longer, so stray light reaches the sensor
The sensor signal is amplified, and random noise is boosted with it
The lens closes its aperture, which lowers overall sharpness
The camera compresses the file more heavily at high ISO values

rubric: Higher ISO amplifies the signal, and the noise along with it.
Distractors mix up ISO with shutter time, aperture or file compression.

items.prompt: Which shutter speed is most likely to freeze a dog running across a field?

options.label: 1 s

rubric: Fast shutter speeds freeze motion.
Slower speeds record the movement as blur.

items.prompt: What is the main idea behind the rule of thirds?

options.label: Dividing the frame into three equal bands means each band should usually hold a different subject
Placing the subject near a corner of the frame usually avoids a dull picture better than other positions
Keeping the horizon in the middle of the frame usually gives the strongest, most stable image
Placing the subject near a grid-line intersection often feels more balanced than centring it

rubric: The rule suggests off-centre placement near thirds lines for balance.
Distractors turn a guideline into a rigid rule or promote centring.

items.prompt: Which description best matches the light just after sunrise or before sunset (golden hour)?

options.label: High sun gives warm, soft light with short shadows
Low sun gives cool, harsh light with almost no shadows
Overcast sky gives strongly directional light and hard shadows
Low sun gives warm, soft light with long shadows

rubric: Low sun angle creates warm colour, softer light and long shadows.
Distractors swap sun height, colour or shadow quality.

items.prompt: Compared with a fast shutter speed, what effects does a much slower shutter speed have? Select all that apply.

options.label: Image noise is reduced to zero
Moving subjects show more blur
More light reaches the sensor
Camera shake becomes more visible
Depth of field becomes shallower

rubric: Slower shutters admit more light, blur motion and reveal handshake.
Shutter speed does not change depth of field and cannot eliminate noise.

items.prompt: You photograph a friend standing off to the side with trees far behind her. Your camera uses only the centre focus point, and you press the shutter with that point on the trees. In the photo the trees are sharp and your friend is soft. What explains this?

options.label: The shutter speed was too fast, which softens subjects that are close to the lens
The camera focused on the spot under the active point, which was the trees
The aperture was too narrow, which blurs subjects nearer the lens than the background
The ISO was too low, so the camera could not pick out your friend to focus on

rubric: The camera focuses on whatever lies under the active focus point.
Distractors blame exposure settings that do not decide where focus lands.

items.prompt: A correct exposure is 1/125 s at f/8, ISO 100. You open the aperture to f/4 and keep ISO 100. Which shutter speed keeps the same exposure?
rubric: f/8 to f/4 is two stops more light, so the shutter must be two stops faster.
1/250 s is one stop only; slower speeds go the wrong way.

items.prompt: Your exposure is correct at ISO 100, f/2.8, 1/200 s. The light then drops by exactly one stop. You want to keep the same aperture and shutter speed. Which ISO restores exposure?

options.label: ISO 400
ISO 200
ISO 800
ISO 50

rubric: One stop more sensitivity means doubling ISO to 200.
ISO 50 goes the wrong way; 400 and 800 overshoot.

items.prompt: You are shooting a mountain landscape and want the flowers a metre away and the peaks at the horizon both sharp. Which aperture is the best starting choice?
rubric: A narrower aperture such as f/11 gives deep depth of field.
Wide apertures give shallow focus and would blur some of the scene.

items.prompt: You will photograph a youth soccer match in bright midday sun. Which setup is most likely to give sharp action shots?

options.label: Shutter 1/1000 s with continuous autofocus
Shutter 1/30 s with single-shot autofocus
Shutter 1/60 s with a very narrow aperture
Shutter 1/15 s with the lowest possible ISO

rubric: Fast shutter plus continuous autofocus follows and freezes moving players.
Slow shutter speeds blur motion, and single-shot focus will not track movement.

items.prompt: In your editing software, a landscape photo has a bright sky that is nearly white, while the land looks fine. Which adjustment is the best first step to bring back cloud detail?

options.label: Raise the shadows slider
Raise the overall exposure slider
Lower the highlights slider
Raise the whites slider

rubric: Lowering highlights darkens the brightest areas and recovers detail.
The other adjustments brighten the image and make the sky worse or alter the wrong tones.

items.prompt: You want a portrait with a strongly blurred background. Which actions help? Select all that apply.

options.label: Move your subject farther from the background
Use a faster shutter speed
Use a wider aperture such as f/2
Lower the ISO to its minimum
Zoom in to a longer focal length

rubric: Wide aperture, longer focal length and more subject-background distance all increase background blur.
Shutter speed and ISO do not control depth of field.

items.prompt: Indoors in a dim room you shoot children playing, handheld, at 1/30 s, f/2.8, ISO 400. The lens is already at its widest aperture and the kids appear blurred. The photos are bright enough. Which change best fixes the blur?

options.label: Keep 1/30 s and add a tripod for stability
Raise ISO to 1600 and use 1/125 s
Lower ISO to 100 and use 1/8 s
Close the aperture to f/8 and keep 1/30 s

rubric: Faster shutter freezes motion, and higher ISO makes up the lost light.
Slower shutters or a tripod do not stop subject movement, and a narrower aperture darkens the shot.

items.prompt: A scene is correctly exposed at f/4, 1/125 s, ISO 400. You close the aperture to f/8 for more depth of field and keep ISO at 400. Which shutter speed keeps the exposure the same?
rubric: f/4 to f/8 is two stops less light, so the shutter must be two stops slower: 1/125 to 1/30.
1/60 is a one-stop error; 1/250 and 1/500 go the wrong way and underexpose.

items.prompt: A cyclist rides across your frame at a steady pace. You want the rider fairly sharp and the background streaked with motion. Which technique fits?

options.label: 1/30 s, camera held still and aimed at the road ahead
1/30 s, camera swinging to follow the rider through the shot
1/2000 s, camera held still and aimed at the road ahead
1/2000 s, camera swinging to follow the rider through the shot

rubric: Panning at a slow shutter speed keeps the moving subject steady relative to the sensor while the background smears.
A still camera at 1/30 blurs the rider, and 1/2000 s freezes the background so no streaks appear.

items.prompt: You shoot a 24mm landscape with flowers 1 m from the camera and mountains far away. You want both acceptably sharp in one frame. Which setup applies the right approach?

options.label: f/2.8, focus on the flowers so the nearest subject is crisp
f/2.8, focus on the mountains so distant detail is critical
f/11, focus exactly on the mountains because infinity is the limit
f/11, focus about a third of the way into the scene

rubric: A small aperture plus focus at a point between near and far uses depth of field behind and in front of the focus plane.
Focusing at infinity wastes the far-side depth of field and leaves the flowers soft; f/2.8 gives too little depth.

items.prompt: In aperture priority on a bright snowfield, your photos come out dull grey. What adjustment applies the right correction?

options.label: Add -1 EV compensation, because bright scenes need less light on the sensor
Raise ISO two stops, because snow reflects too little light for the meter
Close the aperture two stops, because the meter overexposes reflective scenes
Add +1 EV compensation, because the meter renders bright snow as mid-grey

rubric: Meters aim for mid-grey, so bright scenes need positive compensation to look white.
Negative compensation or ISO and aperture changes darken or misapply the fix and deepen the grey result.

items.prompt: You are framing a portrait of a person in profile, looking toward the right side of a 3:2 frame. Using the rule of thirds, where should you place them?

options.label: In the exact centre, so the space on both sides is equal and balanced
On the left third line, leaving open space on the right ahead of their gaze
At the far left edge, so the empty space behind them is as large as possible
On the right third line, so their face points near the edge to add tension

rubric: Placing the subject on a third line and leaving lead room in the gaze direction feels natural and balanced.
Facing the edge feels cramped, and centring or hugging the edge ignores the thirds guideline.

items.prompt: Indoors, handheld at 50mm, f/1.8, ISO 800, 1/30 s, a walking child is blurred though exposure is correct. Which settings give a sharper frame while keeping exposure about the same? Select all that apply.

options.label: 1/8 s at f/1.8 with ISO 100
1/125 s at f/1.8 with ISO 3200
1/250 s at f/1.8 with ISO 6400
1/30 s at f/8 with ISO 800

rubric: Each faster shutter step is offset by a matching ISO increase: two stops for 1/125, three for 1/250.
f/8 at 1/30 underexposes and still blurs; 1/8 s increases blur and ISO 100 only compensates in light.

items.prompt: You photograph a friend at sunset with the sun behind her. Evaluative metering exposes the sky well, but her face is almost black. You want a visible face and still a colourful sky. What is the best next step?

options.label: Switch to centre-weighted metering and keep the same settings for a better balance
Stop down to f/22 so depth of field evens out the contrast between sky and face
Bounce light onto her face with a reflector or fill flash, then expose slightly brighter
Drop ISO to 100 so the shadows on her face recover detail from the sensor

rubric: Fill light reduces the contrast gap, so the face and sky both sit in the sensor's range.
Aperture and ISO changes do not shift the ratio between face and sky, so the face stays dark.

items.prompt: A tripod-mounted landscape at f/22 on a calm day is soft across the frame, though focus was confirmed and the file is not noisy. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: Tripod vibration from tiny air movement, which only shows up at small apertures
A focus error, because very small apertures shift the focus point toward the lens
Diffraction at a very small aperture spreads light and softens the whole frame
Sensor noise, because small apertures force the camera to use a higher ISO setting

rubric: Diffraction softens images at very small apertures regardless of tripod stability.
Calm air, confirmed focus and clean files rule out vibration, focus shift and ISO-driven noise.

items.prompt: A handheld 200mm shot at 1/60 s, f/8, ISO 400 of a static building is streaky in one direction across the frame. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: The focus mode was continuous, which hunts and smears a stationary subject
The aperture was too wide, so depth of field was too shallow for a static scene
The shutter was too slow for the focal length, so hand shake was magnified
The ISO was too low, which reduces the lens's ability to resolve fine detail

rubric: A long lens magnifies shake, and 1/60 is well below the roughly 1/200 guideline.
f/8 gives ample depth of field, ISO does not affect resolution this way, and focus hunting does not produce directional streaks.

items.prompt: A photo looked fine on the camera's LCD in harsh midday sun, but on the computer the sky and a white shirt are blown out with no detail. What best diagnoses the problem?

options.label: The camera's JPEG compression clipped the highlights later, so the exposure itself was acceptable
Bright sun heated the sensor and added exposure that the LCD preview hides from the photographer
The LCD looked darker in glare than the file really was; the histogram would have shown clipping
The sensor recorded correctly, and the computer monitor adds brightness that was never in the file

rubric: Glare makes the LCD look dim, hiding overexposure; the histogram is the reliable check.
The monitor and compression do not invent clipping, and sensor heating does not add exposure.

items.prompt: A portrait places a person in a grey jacket on a third line against a grey brick wall beside a bright window. Viewers say the subject does not stand out. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: The subject sits on a third line, which makes this kind of frame feel off-balance
Subject and wall share tone and texture, and the bright window competes for attention
The frame needs more negative space, so the subject should sit further from the edges
The focal length is too long, which always flattens subjects into their backgrounds

rubric: Weak tonal and colour separation plus a bright competing area pulls the eye away from the subject.
Third-line placement, focal length and negative space do not explain the loss of separation.

items.prompt: A room is lit by warm tungsten lamps and a daylight window. Whatever white balance you choose, part of the image looks wrong. Why?

options.label: The lights differ in colour temperature, so fixing one tints the other
White balance only affects JPEG files, so RAW files keep both colour casts
Tungsten light has no blue content, so no correction can recover true colour
Auto white balance averages the scene and always produces the same orange cast

rubric: One white balance value can neutralise only one light source; the other then shifts the opposite way.
RAW files carry white balance too, auto does not always give orange, and tungsten can be corrected.

items.prompt: A running dog shot at 1/1000 s, f/2.8, ISO 800, single-shot autofocus (AF-S) is soft, with no visible motion blur. Which are likely causes? Select all that apply.

options.label: Focus was locked before the dog moved, so it left the focus plane
At f/2.8 on a close subject, depth of field was thin, so small distance changes lost focus
ISO 800 is too low to capture the dog's detail while it is moving
1/1000 s is too fast and introduces blur in fast-moving subjects

rubric: AF-S locks once, and a thin depth of field at f/2.8 makes any subject movement toward or away from the camera cause misfocus.
Fast shutters reduce blur, and ISO 800 does not limit sharpness for a moving subject.

items.prompt: You shot a RAW portrait at ISO 3200, f/2.8, 1/500 s, and the meter showed about 2 stops under. In editing you raised exposure by +1.5 EV, and now the skin looks muddy with blotchy shadows. What best explains the result?

options.label: RAW files lose colour accuracy whenever exposure is raised in post, so skin tones turn muddy and blotchy
ISO 3200 is above the camera's native range, so noise is baked evenly into every pixel of the file
Underexposure left little signal in the shadows, so brightening amplified the noise and muddied skin
Raising exposure in editing compresses the highlights, and that compression is what turns skin tones muddy

rubric: Underexposed captures have a poor signal-to-noise ratio in shadows, and lifting them amplifies the noise.
RAW exposure lifts do not inherently lose colour, ISO 3200 is within normal range, and raised exposure does not compress highlights this way.

items.prompt: A photographer shoots a moving cyclist at 1/500s, f/2.8, and gets a sharp cyclist but a face that is slightly soft while the cyclist's chest is crisp. The camera was on single-point AF on the chest. Which is the most likely cause?

options.label: The shutter speed of 1/500s was too slow to freeze the cyclist's head, which moves faster than the chest
Diffraction from the narrow effective aperture at f/2.8 softened the finer facial details, unlike the chest
The ISO was set too low, which reduces fine detail and sharpness at wide apertures like f/2.8
The focal plane sat at the chest, and at f/2.8 the depth of field is too thin to keep the face sharp

rubric: Wide aperture at close range gives thin depth of field, so the face falls outside the focal plane.
Distractors blame shutter speed or diffraction, but diffraction affects small apertures, not f/2.8.

items.prompt: Landscape shots at f/22 on a high-resolution sensor look less crisp across the whole frame than shots at f/9, even on a tripod with perfect focus. What best explains this?

options.label: A tripod's stability is reduced at small apertures because exposures run longer
Lens vignetting grows at f/22 and blurs the image corners
Diffraction at very small apertures spreads light and reduces overall resolution
Depth of field shrinks at f/22, so the foreground goes soft

rubric: Diffraction softens the whole image at small apertures, especially on dense sensors.
Depth of field actually increases at f/22, which the second option reverses.

items.prompt: A portrait taken in open shade looks bluish, while the same scene in direct sun looks neutral with the same white balance setting of 5500K. What explains the difference?

options.label: Open shade is lit by blue sky, which has a higher colour temperature than direct sun
Direct sun has a higher colour temperature, so it cancels the camera's warm bias
Shade lowers ISO sensitivity, which shifts colours toward blue
Shade reduces contrast, and low contrast adds a blue cast to skin tones

rubric: Skylight is cooler (higher Kelvin) than sunlight, so a fixed white balance shows a blue cast.
Other options invent a camera or contrast mechanism for colour shifts.

items.prompt: A photographer meters a snowy scene in average mode and the snow looks grey in the result. Which analysis is correct?

options.label: The meter is overexposing because snow reflects too much light into the sensor
The white balance is set too cool, which darkens bright subjects
The meter assumes the scene averages to mid-grey, so it underexposed the bright snow
The aperture was too wide, which dulls bright whites

rubric: Reflective metering renders bright scenes as mid-grey, so positive exposure compensation is needed.
Distractors attribute the grey to white balance or aperture rather than metering logic.

items.prompt: In a street photo, the subject is placed on a third line, but the image still feels unbalanced and cluttered. A bright, sharp lamp post touches the subject's head from behind. Which element most explains the clutter?

options.label: The depth of field is too shallow, so the background context that would anchor the subject is lost
The tangent where the lamp post meets the head pulls the eye away from the subject
The frame has too much empty negative space beside the subject, leaving the composition lopsided
The third-line placement is too rigid here, so centering the subject would have balanced the frame

rubric: Tangents and merges between background objects and subjects create visual confusion.
Rule of thirds placement is not the fault; the distractors misdiagnose placement or space.

items.prompt: A photographer shoots a dim indoor event at 1/60s, f/4, ISO 3200, and many shots show motion blur on gesturing speakers even though the camera is steady and focus is confirmed sharp on the speakers. Which are plausible contributors? Select all that apply.

options.label: ISO 3200 itself causes blur in moving subjects
The camera's image stabilisation only compensates for camera shake, not subject movement
Aperture f/4 is too wide to keep moving hands sharp, so blur comes from lens opening
Subject motion exceeds what 1/60s can freeze

rubric: Stabilisation cannot stop subject motion, and 1/60s is too slow for gestures.
ISO adds noise, not motion blur; background focus would soften everything similarly, not specifically gestures.

items.prompt: A wedding photographer shoots a backlit couple at sunset. With evaluative metering, the sky is rich but the couple are dark silhouettes. She wants visible faces and keeps the sky detail. Her histogram shows the shadows pushed far left with the highlights just below clipping. What is the best diagnosis?

options.label: ISO is set too high, so the sensor crushes shadow tones and a lower ISO would open up the faces
White balance is set for the warm sky, so the faces lose detail until it is matched to skin tones
Scene dynamic range exceeds one exposure, so faces need fill light or a bracketed blend
Aperture is too narrow, so less light reaches the faces and opening up would fix them without clipping the sky

rubric: Histogram with both ends pressed shows a dynamic range problem solved by fill flash, reflector or bracketing.
Distractors blame settings that alter exposure globally, not the contrast ratio.

items.prompt: For a sports shoot in late-afternoon light, criteria are: freeze a sprinter at 1/1000s, keep ISO below 3200, and isolate the runner from a busy background. The lens opens to f/2.8 and f/5.6 is also available. Light allows ISO 1600 at f/2.8 or ISO 6400 at f/5.6. Which choice best meets the criteria?

options.label: f/2.8 at ISO 6400, because a wider aperture always needs a higher ISO to hold 1/1000s
f/5.6 at ISO 1600, because a narrower aperture lowers noise and still holds 1/1000s
f/5.6 at ISO 6400, because the deeper focus keeps the whole sprinting runner sharp
f/2.8 at ISO 1600, because it meets the ISO limit and blurs the background

rubric: Only f/2.8 at ISO 1600 satisfies the ISO cap and background separation.
Distractors misstate the relationship between aperture and ISO or ignore the ISO limit.

items.prompt: Shooting a product for a catalogue, criteria are: edge-to-edge sharpness on a flat object, minimal retouching time, and consistent colour across 200 items. Which workflow best fits?

options.label: Tripod, fixed lighting, manual exposure and white balance, shot at f/8
Handheld with on-camera flash, auto ISO, shot at f/2.8
Handheld, natural window light, auto white balance, shot at f/1.8
Tripod, mixed ambient light, auto exposure, shot at f/16

rubric: Fixed settings and lighting give consistency, and a mid aperture gives sharpness without diffraction.
Distractors vary light or settings per shot or use extreme apertures.

items.prompt: A photographer must choose between shooting RAW and JPEG for a high-contrast wedding where lighting changes constantly, with a same-day delivery of 20 selects. Criteria: recoverable highlights and shadows, and manageable turnaround. Which is best?

options.label: JPEG, because RAW files cannot be batch edited quickly
RAW, with batch presets applied only to the 20 selects
JPEG, because in-camera processing keeps more highlight detail than RAW
RAW, with every frame edited individually before choosing

rubric: RAW gives latitude, and editing only selects keeps turnaround short.
Distractors wrongly claim JPEG retains more data or force an unnecessary workload.

items.prompt: Two edits of the same landscape are compared. Edit A raises global saturation and clarity heavily. Edit B adjusts a local mask on the sky and warms the foreground slightly. The brief asks for a natural look with a clear focal area. Which judgement is best?

options.label: Edit B, since targeted tweaks guide the eye without looking processed
Edit B, since any warming of the foreground matches the natural light of the scene
Edit A, since stronger colour and clarity raise viewer impact across the whole frame
Edit A, since one global edit keeps tones more consistent than several local masks

rubric: Subtle local edits meet both natural look and focal emphasis.
Distractors overvalue strong saturation or claim universal rules.

items.prompt: A photographer wants to portray a busy market's energy. Criteria: show movement, keep one stall owner recognisable. Which technique best satisfies both?

options.label: Wide aperture f/1.4 at 1/500s, so the crowd blurs from shallow depth of field while the owner stays sharp
Panning at 1/30s to follow a passerby, so the moving shopper is sharp against a streaked background
Handheld 1/2000s, which freezes the crowd and the owner equally and shows no sense of motion
Tripod at 1/8s, owner standing still while crowd blurs

rubric: A slow shutter on a tripod blurs moving people while a still subject stays sharp.
Freezing everything loses movement, and the other options lose the owner.

items.prompt: A photo editor reviews a set for a magazine whose criteria are accurate skin tones, a consistent look, and no visible artefacts. Which judgements are sound? Select all that apply.

options.label: Apply one calibrated colour profile across the series
Reject frames with banding from heavy shadow lifting
Match white balance to a grey card from the first frame of each lighting setup
Push clarity to maximum for consistent crispness

rubric: Avoid artefacts, use calibrated colour and reference white balance for consistency.
Maximum clarity creates halos and unnatural skin, which violates the criteria.

items.prompt: A travel photographer at dusk must pick between a handheld shot at ISO 6400, 1/60s, f/2 and a tripod shot at ISO 200, 2s, f/8. The scene has still architecture and a few walking people. Her criteria: maximum image quality for a large print, while keeping people as natural motion trails. Which choice is best?

options.label: The handheld shot, since 1/60s freezes walking people sharply and the wide aperture keeps the print crisp
The tripod shot, since low ISO and deep focus suit large prints and the blur adds motion
The tripod shot, since a 2s exposure at f/8 averages out sensor noise, so ISO barely matters for print quality
The handheld shot, since f/2 gives the best sharpness across the frame and gathers more light than a tripod

rubric: Tripod and low ISO maximise print quality, and a 2s exposure yields trails.
Distractors misjudge that 1/60s freezes walkers, that f/2 is sharpest, or that long exposure removes all noise.

items.prompt: Shooting raw in a high-contrast scene, you want the cleanest shadows while keeping highlight detail recoverable. Which exposure approach best meets both criteria?

options.label: Judge by the camera's JPEG preview alone, since it shows exactly how much highlight detail the raw file holds
Trust evaluative metering at 0 EV, since the meter is calibrated to preserve highlights and shadows equally well
Underexpose by two stops in every scene, since lifting shadows later costs nothing in noise or color quality
Raise exposure until the raw highlight data sits just short of clipping, then pull brightness down in editing

rubric: Exposing as bright as the raw highlights allow gives shadows more signal and less noise, and the extra brightness is removed later.
The JPEG preview and meter are conservative and tuned to a JPEG, not the raw data; routine underexposure adds shadow noise.

items.prompt: A landscape on a 45MP sensor needs foreground rocks at 0.5 m and distant mountains both critically sharp for a large print. Which approach best meets this?

options.label: Shoot once at f/11 focused on the mountains, since foreground softness will not be visible at print size
Shoot once at f/22 focused at the hyperfocal distance, since smaller apertures always increase sharpness overall
Shoot once at f/2.8 focused on the rocks, since the widest aperture gives the lens its best rendering everywhere
Take several frames near f/8 focused from rocks to mountains and blend them, avoiding diffraction softening at small stops

rubric: Focus stacking at a mid aperture gets full depth without the diffraction softening that f/22 causes on a high-resolution sensor.
Distractors assume smaller is always sharper, or that foreground softness will not show in a large print.

items.prompt: A child dances indoors in dim light. You can use ISO 6400 at 1/250 s or ISO 800 at 1/30 s, both at f/2. Judged by freezing the motion and getting a usable image, which is best?

options.label: ISO 6400 at 1/250 s, because some noise is easier to tolerate or clean than motion blur is to remove
ISO 800 at 1/30 s, because lower noise matters more than sharpness for a moving subject
ISO 6400 at 1/250 s, because a higher ISO makes more light reach the sensor and brightens the scene
ISO 800 at 1/30 s, because lens stabilisation will freeze the child's movement during the exposure

rubric: Motion blur is essentially unrecoverable while noise can be reduced, so the faster shutter wins.
Stabilisation only corrects camera shake, and ISO amplifies the signal rather than gathering more light.

items.prompt: Indoors with a white ceiling 3 m high, you want soft, flattering portrait light from one speedlight. Which judgement is best?

options.label: Aim it at a black wall to absorb spill, since absorbed light gives a gentler look on the face
Aim it straight at the face and lower the power, since less output makes the light itself softer
Fit a small diffuser dome and fire direct, since the dome enlarges the source enough to soften shadows
Bounce the flash off the ceiling or a nearby white wall, since a large reflecting surface softens shadows

rubric: Softness depends on the apparent source size, so a big bounce surface gives soft light.
Lower power does not change hardness, a small dome barely enlarges the source, and a black wall gives almost no light.

items.prompt: A photographer delivers the same images for web and for gallery prints and needs colour to match expectations in both. Which workflow is best?

options.label: Edit on a calibrated monitor, export sRGB for web, and soft-proof with the printer's paper profile before printing
Embed no colour profile on any export, since untagged files appear identical on every screen and printer
Edit by eye on a laptop at full brightness, then rely on the print lab to correct whatever looks different
Edit on any bright screen, then export everything in the widest gamut, since every display and printer will show it

rubric: Calibration, a safe web space and soft-proofing manage colour predictably across devices.
Wide gamut and untagged files display inconsistently, and uncalibrated editing gives unreliable judgements.

items.prompt: A portrait is backlit by a bright sky, and evaluative metering leaves the face dark. Which judgements about fixing it are sound? Select all that apply.

options.label: Add fill flash or a reflector to lift the face toward the sky's brightness
Stop down to f/16 so the face rises to the sky's exposure level
Spot-meter the face and accept a brighter, partly clipped sky if the face is the priority
Lower the ISO so the sensor records more shadow detail in the face
Dial in negative exposure compensation to brighten the face

rubric: Metering for the face or adding fill reduces the contrast gap, which is the real problem.
Stopping down, lowering ISO or using negative compensation darkens or leaves the face unchanged.

items.prompt: At dawn you track a heron in flight with a 400mm f/5.6 lens. Light is weak, and wingbeats blur at 1/500 s. Your camera is clean to ISO 6400 and acceptable at 12800. Which setup best delivers frozen wings in a usable file?

options.label: Shutter 1/1000 s at f/16 and ISO 6400, since stopping down sharpens the wings and offsets motion
Aperture priority at f/5.6 with ISO fixed at 800, since a cleaner file outweighs a few blurred wingtips
Manual 1/2000 s at f/5.6 with auto ISO up to 12800, accepting noise and cleaning it in editing
Shutter 1/60 s at ISO 200 on a tripod, since the tripod steadies the lens and freezes wing motion

rubric: A fast shutter is the priority for frozen wings, and the noise cost is acceptable within the camera's range.
A tripod does not stop subject motion, and fixed low ISO or small apertures only produce blur or darkness.

items.prompt: Design a Milky Way exposure on a full-frame body with a 24mm f/2.8 lens. Constraints: stars stay points (about 500 divided by focal length in seconds) and noise is low. Which plan meets both?

options.label: Many 15 to 20 s frames at f/2.8 and ISO 3200, aligned and stacked to reduce noise
One 5 s frame at f/2.8 and ISO 12800, since the short shutter stops trailing and raw files hide noise
One 20 s exposure at f/8 and ISO 400, since stopping down keeps stars small and noise low
One 60 s exposure at f/2.8 and ISO 1600, since a longer shutter reduces noise without visible trailing

rubric: Short frames keep stars as points, and stacking many frames averages out noise.
60 s trails stars at 24mm, f/8 at ISO 400 is far too dark, and a single ISO 12800 frame is noisy.

items.prompt: Design a headshot setup with one speedlight in a small room. Constraints: soft light, a visible catchlight, and no hard shadow on the wall behind the subject. Which plan meets every constraint?

options.label: Put a large softbox close at about 45 degrees, subject well away from the wall, reflector as fill
Put a bare flash far to the side at head height, with the subject against the wall so the shadow hides behind them
Put a small grid on the flash close to the face, with the subject touching the wall so any shadows vanish
Mount the bare flash on the camera aimed straight at the face, with the subject against the wall for a clean look

rubric: A large close source is soft and makes a catchlight, and distance from the wall keeps shadows off it.
Bare, gridded or on-camera flash is hard, and a subject near the wall casts visible shadows on it.

items.prompt: Design one frame that conveys a canyon's vastness using a lone hiker. Constraints: the hiker is readable, scale is obvious, and the eye is led through the frame. Which plan fits?

options.label: Place the hiker large at the bottom with the canyon cropped out, so the hiker's size implies scale and fills the frame
Shoot wide with the hiker small near a third line, canyon lines leading to them, foreground sharp
Use a telephoto close crop on the hiker's face so the canyon shows only as a blurred background, keeping the figure readable
Shoot the canyon wide with no figure and a centred horizon, so the symmetry of the walls gives balanced scale

rubric: A small figure against large forms with leading lines gives readable scale and a path for the eye.
The other plans remove the canyon or the human reference that makes scale readable.

items.prompt: Design a sunrise time-lapse running from darkness to full sun on one camera, with no visible flicker. Which plan best meets this?

options.label: Aperture priority with auto ISO, letting the camera choose each frame so brightness follows the scene smoothly
Manual mode, fixed aperture and white balance, ramping shutter and ISO in small steps, then smoothing in post
Auto white balance and metering with bracketing on each frame, merging every bracket into an HDR frame to hold exposure steady
Fixed 1/60 s, f/8 and ISO 100 for every frame, then brightening the dark frames in editing to even out the sequence

rubric: Manual control with gradual ramping avoids frame-to-frame jumps, and a fixed aperture avoids flicker.
Auto modes vary per frame, and fixed settings cannot span the huge brightness range.

items.prompt: Design a workflow to deliver 800 wedding photos shot in mixed lighting (church, outdoors, reception) in a consistent style within 48 hours. Which plan fits?

options.label: Edit each photo from scratch in the order shot, so every frame gets individual attention and nothing is shared
Apply one preset with identical values to all frames, since the same numbers guarantee the same colour everywhere
Edit only the 50 best photos in detail and deliver the others straight from camera JPEGs
Cull first, apply a base look, sync white balance per lighting group, then hand-polish only the hero images

rubric: Culling, a shared look and group-wise corrections give consistency at scale, with time kept for key images.
One preset ignores changing light, and per-frame editing or JPEG delivery breaks the deadline or style.

items.prompt: Design a macro shoot of a ring at 1:1 needing sharpness front to back, minimal diffraction and no harsh reflections. Which plan elements meet the constraints? Select all that apply.

options.label: A light tent or diffusion around the ring
A single shot at f/32 for full depth of field
Direct bare flash from the camera
Focus stacking on a macro rail at about f/8
A tripod with remote release and mirror lock-up

rubric: Stacking, diffusion and a stable setup deliver depth, soft reflections and sharpness.
f/32 causes severe diffraction at 1:1, and bare flash creates harsh reflections.

items.prompt: A planner proposes a plan for a dim wedding dance floor: off-camera flash on a stand, ISO 800, f/4, 1/200 s, manual, raw. The goal is frozen dancers and a visibly lit venue behind them. What is the plan missing?

options.label: A slower shutter around 1/30 s, so ambient light registers while the flash freezes the dancers
A smaller aperture of f/16, since it extends flash range and brightens the background
A faster shutter such as 1/1000 s, since it brings in more ambient light for the venue
More flash power alone, since it will light the backdrop as well as the dancers

rubric: Flash power freezes the subject but shutter speed controls ambient, so dragging the shutter exposes the venue.
Faster shutters and smaller apertures reduce ambient light, and more power does not light the distant background.
